headline: Illegal Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs found inside state-owned China Telecom's network
summary: An Israeli security firm identified 32 Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 chips within China Telecom's network, despite strict U.S. export controls banning their sale to China.
details: An Israeli security firm, Lava, has identified 32 Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 chips operating within the network of China Telecom, a state-owned company. These high-powered chips are subject to strict U.S. export controls, raising questions about their presence in China.

The Blackwell Ultra B300 is one of the most powerful data center GPUs globally, announced in March last year with significant performance gains and increased memory over its predecessor, the B200. It is designed for sophisticated AI LLMs and was expected to ship by the end of 2025.

This incident follows previous reports of widespread smuggling, with Chinese companies reportedly illicitly acquiring $1 billion worth of Nvidia AI chips in just three months in 2025. In August 2026, nine individuals were indicted in Taiwan for illegally exporting B300 GPUs to China, shortly after Supermicro fired employees over a smuggling investigation.

Lava detected the B300 chips using Nvidia's DCGM Exporter tool, a monitoring software often accessible beyond data center networks and sometimes without password authentication. Nvidia has acknowledged working on a tool to locate its chips but has not yet released it.

Nvidia downplayed the report, stating that the diversion of controlled U.S. products is "insignificant," less than half of one percent in recent court cases. A spokesperson claimed smuggling is a "nonfactor" compared to China's existing domestic compute resources.

The intense demand for Nvidia's AI chips has driven up prices for even older silicon, with five-year-old A100 servers tripling in cost to up to $82,000. This scarcity has led some firms to retool gaming GPUs to handle AI workloads where possible.
